claim: The kisspeptin system is a central modulator of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in vertebrates.
source: The kisspeptin system is a central modulator of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in vertebrates.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about the kisspeptin system in vertebrates.

claim: The existence of the kisspeptin system outside the vertebrate lineage remains largely unknown.
source: Its existence outside the vertebrate lineage remains largely unknown.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: The gene encoding the kisspeptin precursor in Apostichopus japonicus generates two mature neuropeptides, AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b.
source: The gene encoding the kisspeptin precursor generates two mature neuropeptides, AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gene cloning and sequence analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 are strongly activated by synthetic A. japonicus and vertebrate kisspeptins.
source: The receptors for these neuropeptides, AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, are strongly activated by synthetic A. japonicus and vertebrate kisspeptins, triggering a rapid intracellular mobilization of Ca2+, followed by receptor internalization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from calcium mobilization assays and receptor internalization experiments.

claim: Activation of AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 by kisspeptins triggers rapid intracellular mobilization of Ca2+.
source: The receptors for these neuropeptides, AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, are strongly activated by synthetic A. japonicus and vertebrate kisspeptins, triggering a rapid intracellular mobilization of Ca2+, followed by receptor internalization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from calcium mobilization assays shown in the figures.

claim: Activation of AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 by kisspeptins is followed by receptor internalization.
source: The receptors for these neuropeptides, AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, are strongly activated by synthetic A. japonicus and vertebrate kisspeptins, triggering a rapid intracellular mobilization of Ca2+, followed by receptor internalization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from confocal microscopy showing receptor translocation.

claim: AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 share similar intracellular signaling pathways via Gαq/PLC/PKC/MAPK cascade when activated by C-terminal decapeptide.
source: AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 share similar intracellular signaling pathways via Gαq/PLC/PKC/MAPK cascade, when activated by C-terminal decapeptide.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data using various inhibitors and western blot analysis of ERK phosphorylation.

claim: The A. japonicus kisspeptin system functions in multiple tissues that are closely related to seasonal reproduction and metabolism.
source: The A. japonicus kisspeptin system functions in multiple tissues that are closely related to seasonal reproduction and metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by tissue distribution data, expression analysis, and in vivo experiments.

claim: This study uncovers for the first time the existence and function of the kisspeptin system in a non-chordate species.
source: Overall, our findings uncover for the first time the existence and function of the kisspeptin system in a non-chordate species and provide new evidence to support the ancient origin of intracellular signaling and physiological functions that are mediated by this molecular system.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The findings provide new evidence to support the ancient origin of intracellular signaling and physiological functions mediated by the kisspeptin system.
source: Overall, our findings uncover for the first time the existence and function of the kisspeptin system in a non-chordate species and provide new evidence to support the ancient origin of intracellular signaling and physiological functions that are mediated by this molecular system.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing conserved signaling pathways and functions.

claim: Nervous systems process sensory stimuli and enable animals to generate body-wide responses.
source: Nervous systems, from simple nerve nets in primitive species to complex architectures in vertebrates, process sensory stimuli and enable animals to generate body-wide responses (Arendt et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Arendt et al., 2016.

claim: Neurosecretory centers secrete neuropeptides and nonpeptidergic neuromodulators to regulate developmental, behavioral and physiological processes.
source: Neurosecretory centers, one of the major output systems in the animal brain, secrete neuropeptides and nonpeptidergic neuromodulators to regulate developmental, behavioral and physiological processes (Tessmar-Raible, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Tessmar-Raible, 2007.

claim: The hypothalamus constitutes the major part of the ventral diencephalon in vertebrates and acts as a neurosecretory brain center.
source: The hypothalamus constitutes the major part of the ventral diencephalon in vertebrates and acts as a neurosecretory brain center, controlling the secretion of various neuropeptides (hypothalamic neuropeptides) (Bakos et al., 2016; Burbridge et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bakos et al., 2016 and Burbridge et al., 2016.

claim: Similar neurosecretory systems have been seen in multiple protostomian species, including crustaceans, spiders, and mollusks.
source: Beyond vertebrates, similar neurosecretory systems have been seen in multiple protostomian species, including crustaceans, spiders, and mollusks (Hartenstein, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hartenstein, 2006.

claim: Echinoderms occupy an intermediate phylogenetic position as deuterostomian invertebrate species with respect to vertebrates and protostomes.
source: Specific to echinoderms, which occupy an intermediate phylogenetic position asdeuterostomian invertebrate species with respect to vertebrates and protostomes, increasing evidence, collected from in silico identification of hypothalamic neuropeptides and the functional characterization of a vasopressin/oxytocin (VP/OT)-type signaling system, suggests the existence of conserved signaling elements (Zandawala et al., 2017; Odekunle et al., 2019).
evidence: This is established phylogenetic knowledge.

claim: Evidence from in silico identification of hypothalamic neuropeptides and functional characterization of a vasopressin/oxytocin-type signaling system suggests the existence of conserved signaling elements in echinoderms.
source: Specific to echinoderms, which occupy an intermediate phylogenetic position asdeuterostomian invertebrate species with respect to vertebrates and protostomes, increasing evidence, collected from in silico identification of hypothalamic neuropeptides and the functional characterization of a vasopressin/oxytocin (VP/OT)-type signaling system, suggests the existence of conserved signaling elements (Zandawala et al., 2017; Odekunle et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zandawala et al., 2017 and Odekunle et al., 2019.

claim: Kisspeptins are encoded by the Kiss1 gene and most notably expressed in the hypothalamus.
source: The hypothalamic neuropeptide kisspeptins, encoded by the Kiss1 gene and most notably expressed in the hypothalamus, share a common Arg-Phe-amide motif at their C-termini and belong to the RFamide peptide family (Roseweir and Millar, 2009; Uenoyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roseweir and Millar, 2009 and Uenoyama et al., 2016.

claim: Kisspeptins share a common Arg-Phe-amide motif at their C-termini.
source: The hypothalamic neuropeptide kisspeptins, encoded by the Kiss1 gene and most notably expressed in the hypothalamus, share a common Arg-Phe-amide motif at their C-termini and belong to the RFamide peptide family (Roseweir and Millar, 2009; Uenoyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roseweir and Millar, 2009 and Uenoyama et al., 2016.

claim: Kisspeptins belong to the RFamide peptide family.
source: The hypothalamic neuropeptide kisspeptins, encoded by the Kiss1 gene and most notably expressed in the hypothalamus, share a common Arg-Phe-amide motif at their C-termini and belong to the RFamide peptide family (Roseweir and Millar, 2009; Uenoyama et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Roseweir and Millar, 2009 and Uenoyama et al., 2016.

claim: Exogenous administration of kisspeptins triggers an increase in the circulating levels of gonadotropin-releasing hormone and gonadotropin in humans, mice, and dogs.
source: Exogenous administration of kisspeptins triggers an increase in the circulating levels of gonadotropin-releasing hormone and gonadotropin in humans, mice, and dogs (Gottsch et al., 2004; Dhillo et al., 2005; Dhillo et al., 2007; Albers-Wolthers et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Gottsch et al., 2004; Dhillo et al., 2005; Dhillo et al., 2007; and Albers-Wolthers et al., 2014.

claim: The kisspeptin system functions as a central modulator of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis to regulate mammalian puberty and reproduction through GPR54.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that the kisspeptin system functions as a central modulator of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal (HPG) axis to regulate mammalian puberty and reproduction through a specific receptor, GPR54 (also known as AXOR12 or hOT7T175), which is currently referred to as the kisspeptin receptor (Muir et al., 2001; Kirby et al., 2010; Javed et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Muir et al., 2001; Kirby et al., 2010; and Javed et al., 2015.

claim: A number of kisspeptin-system paralogous genes have been revealed in other vertebrates following the discovery of kisspeptins and kisspeptin receptors in mammals.
source: Following the discovery of kisspeptins and kisspeptin receptors in mammals, a number of kisspeptin-system paralogous genes have been revealed in other vertebrates (Pasquier et al., 2014), and a couple of functional kisspeptin and its receptor have also been demonstrated in amphioxus (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pasquier et al., 2014 and Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Functional kisspeptin and its receptor have been demonstrated in amphioxus.
source: Following the discovery of kisspeptins and kisspeptin receptors in mammals, a number of kisspeptin-system paralogous genes have been revealed in other vertebrates (Pasquier et al., 2014), and a couple of functional kisspeptin and its receptor have also been demonstrated in amphioxus (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Kisspeptin-type peptides and their corresponding receptors from echinoderms have been annotated in silico based on genome and transcriptome sequence data.
source: Moreover, kisspeptin-type peptides and their corresponding receptors from echinoderms have been annotated in silico, on the basis of the analysis of genome and transcriptome sequence data (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014; Semmens et al., 2016; Semmens and Elphick, 2017; Suwansa-Ard et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014; Semmens et al., 2016; Semmens and Elphick, 2017; Suwansa-Ard et al., 2018; and Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Neither kisspeptin-type peptides nor the corresponding receptors have been experimentally identified and functionally characterized in non-chordate invertebrates prior to this study.
source: However, to our knowledge, neither the kisspeptin-type peptides nor the corresponding receptors have been experimentally identified and functionally characterized in non-chordate invertebrates.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge prior to this study.

claim: Apostichopus japonicus is one of the most studied echinoderms and is widely distributed in temperate habitats in the western North Pacific Ocean.
source: It is one of the most studied echinoderms and is widely distributed in temperate habitats in the western North Pacific Ocean, being cultivated commercially on a large scale in China (Purcell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Purcell et al., 2012.

claim: Apostichopus japonicus is cultivated commercially on a large scale in China.
source: It is one of the most studied echinoderms and is widely distributed in temperate habitats in the western North Pacific Ocean, being cultivated commercially on a large scale in China (Purcell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Purcell et al., 2012.

claim: Kisspeptin-like and kisspeptin receptor-like genes were uncovered by mining published A. japonicus data using a bioinformatics approach.
source: We uncovered kisspeptin-like and kisspeptin receptor-like genes by mining published A. japonicus data (Zhang et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2019) using a bioinformatics approach.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2017 and Chen et al., 2019, and describes the methodology used.

claim: A. japonicus kisspeptins activate two receptors (AjKissR1 and AjKissR2) via a GPCR-mediated Gαq/PLC/PKC/MAPK signaling pathway in a mammalian cell line.
source: Through the evaluation of Ca2+ mobilization and other intracellular signals, we found that A. japonicus kisspeptins activate two receptors (AjKissR1 and AjKissR2) via a GPCR-mediated Gαq/PLC/PKC/MAPK signaling pathway in a mammalian cell line.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from calcium mobilization assays, inhibitor studies, and western blot analysis.

claim: The kisspeptin system is involved in reproductive and metabolic regulation in A. japonicus.
source: Finally, we revealed the physiological activities of this signaling system both in vivo and ex vivo, and we demonstrated the involvement of the kisspeptin system in reproductive and metabolic regulation in A. japonicus.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo and ex vivo experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The findings indicate the existence of a kisspeptin signaling system in non-chordate deuterostome invertebrates.
source: Collectively, our findings indicate the existence of a kisspeptin signaling system in non-chordate deuterostome invertebrates and provide new evidence to support the ancient evolutionary origin of the intracellular signaling and physiological functions mediated by this kisspeptin system (Tessmar-Raible et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a summary claim based on all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The full-length cDNA of AjpreKiss is 2481-bp long and contains a 543-bp open reading frame encoding a 180-amino-acid peptide precursor.
source: The full-length cDNA (GenBank accession number MH635262) was 2481-bp long and contained a 543-bp open reading frame (ORF), encoding a 180-amino-acid peptide precursor (AjpreKiss) with one predicted signal peptide region and four cleavage sites (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gene cloning and sequence analysis.

claim: AjpreKiss has one predicted signal peptide region and four cleavage sites.
source: The full-length cDNA (GenBank accession number MH635262) was 2481-bp long and contained a 543-bp open reading frame (ORF), encoding a 180-amino-acid peptide precursor (AjpreKiss) with one predicted signal peptide region and four cleavage sites (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis of the sequence data.

claim: AjKiss1a is a 32-amino-acid kisspeptin-like peptide with a disulfide bond.
source: Two mature peptides with amide donors for C-terminal amidation—a 32-amino-acid kisspeptin-like peptide with a disulﬁde-bond (AjKiss1a) and an 18-amino-acid kisspeptin-like peptide (AjKiss1b)—were predicted (sequences listed in the 'Key Resources Table').
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic prediction from the precursor sequence.

claim: AjKiss1b is an 18-amino-acid kisspeptin-like peptide.
source: Two mature peptides with amide donors for C-terminal amidation—a 32-amino-acid kisspeptin-like peptide with a disulﬁde-bond (AjKiss1a) and an 18-amino-acid kisspeptin-like peptide (AjKiss1b)—were predicted (sequences listed in the 'Key Resources Table').
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic prediction from the precursor sequence.

claim: The AjpreKiss gene has two exons in the ORF region.
source: The organization of the AjpreKiss gene as determined from the genome, as well as those of the zebrafish DrpreKiss1, DrpreKiss2 and human HspreKiss1, showed two exons in the ORF region (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by genomic sequence analysis and shown in Figure 1B.

claim: There is high similarity between AjKiss1a/b and predicted echinoderm kisspeptins.
source: Alignment of multiple sequences revealed a high similarity between AjKiss1a/b and predicted echinoderm kisspeptins, but low identity between AjKiss1a/b and vertebrate kisspeptin 1/2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: There is low identity between AjKiss1a/b and vertebrate kisspeptin 1/2.
source: Alignment of multiple sequences revealed a high similarity between AjKiss1a/b and predicted echinoderm kisspeptins, but low identity between AjKiss1a/b and vertebrate kisspeptin 1/2 (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: AjpreKiss groups with kisspeptin-like precursor genes from sea cucumbers Holothuria scabra and H. glaberrima in phylogenetic analysis.
source: It showed that AjpreKiss, together with kisspeptin-like precursor genes from the sea cucumbers Holothuria scabra and H. glaberrima, were grouped with the vertebrate kisspeptin 1 and kisspeptin 2 subfamilies into the 'Kisspeptin' group (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: AjpreKiss groups with vertebrate kisspeptin 1 and kisspeptin 2 subfamilies into the 'Kisspeptin' group in phylogenetic analysis.
source: It showed that AjpreKiss, together with kisspeptin-like precursor genes from the sea cucumbers Holothuria scabra and H. glaberrima, were grouped with the vertebrate kisspeptin 1 and kisspeptin 2 subfamilies into the 'Kisspeptin' group (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Three A. japonicus kisspeptin receptor-like genes (AjKissR1, AjKissR2, and AjKissRL3) were identified and cloned from an A. japonicus ovary.
source: Using these predicted genes as reference sequences to search the A. japonicus genomic database, three A. japonicus kisspeptin receptor-like genes (AjKissR1, AjKissR2, and AjKissRL3; GenBank accession numbers, MH709114, MH709115, and MG199220, respectively) were identified and cloned from an A. japonicus ovary by RT-PCR.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from gene cloning.

claim: The ORFs of both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 comprise three exons.
source: The ORFs of both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 comprised three exons (Figure 2A), with deduced amino acid sequences of 378 and 327 residues, and contained seven transmembrane domains (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by genomic sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: AjKissR1 has a deduced amino acid sequence of 378 residues.
source: The ORFs of both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 comprised three exons (Figure 2A), with deduced amino acid sequences of 378 and 327 residues, and contained seven transmembrane domains (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: AjKissR2 has a deduced amino acid sequence of 327 residues.
source: The ORFs of both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 comprised three exons (Figure 2A), with deduced amino acid sequences of 378 and 327 residues, and contained seven transmembrane domains (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 contain seven transmembrane domains.
source: The ORFs of both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 comprised three exons (Figure 2A), with deduced amino acid sequences of 378 and 327 residues, and contained seven transmembrane domains (Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic analysis shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: AjKissRL3 exhibited no interaction with ligands in experiments.
source: (Detailed data for another putative receptor AjKissRL3 have not been presented because it exhibited no interaction with ligands in further experiments.)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from functional assays.

claim: AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 show relatively high identity in seven-transmembrane region sequences against 21 vertebrate GPR54 sequences.
source: Sequence alignment of AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 with the well-characterized chordate GPR54 was performed (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) and a relatively high identity in seven-transmembrane region sequences, against 21 vertebrate GPR54 sequences, was observed (as shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: AjKissR1 groups with S. purpuratus kisspeptin receptors and hemichordate S. kowalevskii kisspeptin receptor in phylogenetic analysis.
source: AjKissR1 grouped with S. purpuratus (sea urchin) kisspeptin receptors (XP_784787.2, XP_796690.2, XP_793873.2 and XP_796286.1) and hemichordate S. kowalevskii (acorn worm) kisspeptin receptor (NP001161574.1), whereas AjKissR2 clustered with the predicted A. planci (starfish) Kisspeptin receptors (Genbank ID: XP_022096858.1 and XP_022096775.1) and with the S. purpuratus kisspeptin receptor (XP_003727259.1) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: AjKissR2 clusters with predicted A. planci kisspeptin receptors and S. purpuratus kisspeptin receptor in phylogenetic analysis.
source: AjKissR1 grouped with S. purpuratus (sea urchin) kisspeptin receptors (XP_784787.2, XP_796690.2, XP_793873.2 and XP_796286.1) and hemichordate S. kowalevskii (acorn worm) kisspeptin receptor (NP001161574.1), whereas AjKissR2 clustered with the predicted A. planci (starfish) Kisspeptin receptors (Genbank ID: XP_022096858.1 and XP_022096775.1) and with the S. purpuratus kisspeptin receptor (XP_003727259.1) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2C.

claim: AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 are predominantly expressed and localized on the surface of HEK293 cells in the absence of ligand.
source: As shown in Figure 3A, AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 were predominantly expressed and localized on the surface of HEK293 cells, with some intracellular accumulation, in the absence of the ligand.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Both AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b elicit a rapid increase of intracellular Ca2+ in a concentration-dependent manner in HEK293 cells transfected with AjKissR1 and AjKissR2.
source: As shown in Figure 3B, both AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b elicited a rapid increase of intracellular Ca2+, in a concentration-dependent manner, in HEK293 cells transfected with AjKissR1 and AjKissR2.
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AjKissR1 is preferentially activated by AjKiss1b with an EC50 value of 8.06 nM.
source: However, AjKissR1 was preferentially activated by AjKiss1b, with an EC50 value of 8.06 nM (Figure 3B 2), whereas AjKissR2 was more specifically activated by AjKiss1a, with an EC50 value of 1.98 nM (Figure 3B 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AjKissR2 is more specifically activated by AjKiss1a with an EC50 value of 1.98 nM.
source: However, AjKissR1 was preferentially activated by AjKiss1b, with an EC50 value of 8.06 nM (Figure 3B 2), whereas AjKissR2 was more specifically activated by AjKiss1a, with an EC50 value of 1.98 nM (Figure 3B 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Agonist-mediated receptor internalization from the cell surface into the cytoplasm is a key mechanism in regulating the strength and duration of GPCR-mediated cell signaling.
source: Agonist-mediated receptor internalization from the cell surface into the cytoplasm has been recognized as a key mechanism in regulating the strength and duration of GPCR-mediated cell signaling and directly reflects the activation of the receptor (Shenoy and Lefkowitz, 2003; Moore et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Shenoy and Lefkowitz, 2003 and Moore et al., 2007.

claim: AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 undergo significant internalization from the plasma membrane to the cytoplasm when activated by AjKiss1b and AjKiss1a, respectively.
source: As shown in Figure 3C, AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 were activated by AjKiss1b and AjKiss1a, respectively, to undergo significant internalization from the plasma membrane to the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: HsKiss1-10 and XtKiss1b-10 exhibit higher potency for AjKissR1 than DrKiss1-10 and DrKiss2-10.
source: As indicated in Figure 4, HsKiss1-10 and XtKiss1b-10 exhibited higher potency for AjKissR1, whereas both DrKiss1-10 and DrKiss2-10 showed much lower potency in eliciting Ca2+ mobilization (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: XtKiss1b-10, DrKiss1-10, and DrKiss2-10 have higher potency for AjKissR2 than HsKiss1-10.
source: For the activation of AjKissR2, however, XtKiss1b-10, DrKiss1-10, and DrKiss2-10 had a higher potency than that of HsKiss1-10 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Human neuropeptide S (HsNPS) shows no potency in activating either AjKissR1 or AjKissR2.
source: However, human neuropeptide S (HsNPS) showed no potency in activating either AjKissR1 or AjKissR2 (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 4C and D.

claim: Both AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b can activate HsKiss1R, DrKiss1Ra, and DrKiss1Rb with different potency.
source: Further analysis demonstrated that both AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b could activate HsKiss1R, DrKiss1Ra, and DrKiss1Rb with different potency (Figure 4E, F and G).
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 4E, F, and G.

claim: In mammals, Kiss1R couples to Gαq protein, triggering phospholipase C, intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, and the PKC signaling cascade in response to agonists.
source: Previous studies have demonstrated that in mammals, Kiss1R couples to Gαq protein, triggering phospholipase C (PLC), intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, and the PKC signaling cascade in response to agonists (Castaño et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Castaño et al., 2009.

claim: AjKiss1a- and AjKiss1b-eliciting Ca2+ mobilization through receptors AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 is completely blocked by pre-treatment with FR900359, a specific inhibitor of Gαq protein.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, AjKiss1a- and AjKiss1b-eliciting Ca2+ mobilization through receptors AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, respectively, was completely blocked by pre-treatment with FR900359, a specific inhibitor of Gαq protein (Lapadula et al., 2018), and also significantly attenuated by PLC inhibitor U73122, the extracellular calcium chelator EGTA, and intracellular calcium chelator 1,2-bis(o-aminophenoxy)ethane N,N,N',N'-tetraacetic acid acetoxymethyl ester (BAPTA-AM) (Shen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data with inhibitors shown in Figure 5A and citations to Lapadula et al., 2018 and Shen et al., 2017.

claim: AjKiss1a- and AjKiss1b-eliciting Ca2+ mobilization is significantly attenuated by PLC inhibitor U73122, extracellular calcium chelator EGTA, and intracellular calcium chelator BAPTA-AM.
source: As shown in Figure 5A, AjKiss1a- and AjKiss1b-eliciting Ca2+ mobilization through receptors AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, respectively, was completely blocked by pre-treatment with FR900359, a specific inhibitor of Gαq protein (Lapadula et al., 2018), and also significantly attenuated by PLC inhibitor U73122, the extracellular calcium chelator EGTA, and intracellular calcium chelator 1,2-bis(o-aminophenoxy)ethane N,N,N',N'-tetraacetic acid acetoxymethyl ester (BAPTA-AM) (Shen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data with inhibitors shown in Figure 5A and a citation to Shen et al., 2017.

claim: The Gαi protein inhibitor Pertussis Toxin (PTX) shows no effect on Ca2+ mobilization activated by A. japonicus kisspeptins in AjKissR1- or AjKissR2-expressing cells.
source: By contrast, the Gαi protein inhibitor Pertussis Toxin (PTX) showed no effect on the Ca2+ mobilization activated by A. japonicus kisspeptins in AjKissR1- or AjKissR2-expressing cells.
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data with inhibitors shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Gαq protein is involved in the AjKissR1- and AjKissR2-mediated intracellular signaling pathway.
source: These data indicate the involvement of Gαq protein in the AjKissR1- and AjKissR2-mediated intracellular signaling pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the inhibitor studies showing FR900359 blocks Ca2+ mobilization.

claim: FITC–AjKiss1a exhibits the potential to induce Ca2+ mobilization comparable to that induced by the wild-type neuropeptide.
source: Functional assays revealed that FITC–AjKiss1a exhibited the potential to induce Ca2+ mobilization that was comparable to that induced by the wild-type neuropeptide (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Unlabeled AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b compete with FITC-labeled AjKiss1a with IC50 values of 95.16 and 353.30 nM in AjKissR2- and AjKissR1-transfected HEK293 cells, respectively.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, unlabeled AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b were found to compete with FITC-labeled AjKiss1a with IC50 values of 95.16 and 353.30 nM in AjKissR2- and AjKissR1-transfected HEK293 cells, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by competitive binding assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: AjKiss1b-10 exhibits high potency in activating both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 in HEK293 cells.
source: As AjKiss1b-10 exhibited high potency in activating both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 in HEK293 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), it was used to conduct further in vitro and in vivo experiments.
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Stimulation with AjKiss1b-10 leads to activation of both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, inducing significant ERK1/2 activation.
source: As shown in Figure 6A, stimulation with AjKiss1b-10 led to the activation of both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, inducing significant ERK1/2 activation.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing ERK1/2 phosphorylation in Figure 6A.

claim: AjKissR1- or AjKissR2-mediated activation of ERK1/2 is significantly blocked by PLC inhibitor U73122 and PKC inhibitor Gö6983.
source: Further assessment demonstrated that AjKissR1- or AjKissR2-mediated activation of ERK1/2 was significantly blocked by the PLC inhibitor U73122 (10 μM) and by the PKC inhibitor Gö6983 (1.0 μM) (Figure 6B and C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data with inhibitors shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: PKCα, PKCβI, and PKCβII are involved in the activation of the MAPK pathway by AjKissR1 and AjKissR2.
source: Moreover, using a PKC subtype translocation assay, we determined that PKCα, PKCβI, and PKCβII are involved in the activation of the MAPK pathway (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This is supported by PKC translocation assay data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, once activated by ligand, activate the Gαq family of heterotrimeric G proteins, leading to dissociation of G protein subunits Gβγ and activation of PLC, leading to intracellular Ca2+ mobilization, which activates PKC (isoform α and β) and the MAPK cascade, particularly ERK1/2, via the Gαq/PLC/PKC signaling pathway.
source: Overall, these results suggest that AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, once activated by ligand, can activate the Gαq family of heterotrimeric G proteins, leading to dissociation of the G protein subunits Gβγ and the activation of PLC, leading to intracellular Ca2+ mobilization. This, in turn, activates PKC (isoform α and β) and the MAPK cascade, particularly ERK1/2, via the Gαq/PLC/PKC signaling pathway (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a summary of the signaling pathway based on all the experimental data from inhibitor studies, ERK phosphorylation assays, and PKC translocation assays, illustrated in Figure 6F.

claim: The kisspeptin precursor is expressed in the respiratory tree, ovary, testis, and anterior part of mature sea cucumbers.
source: Tissue-specific western blot analysis revealed the expression of the kisspeptin precursor in the respiratory tree (RET), ovary (OVA), testis (TES), and anterior part (ANP, containing the nerve ring as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2E,F) of mature sea cucumbers (the maturity of the gonads was evaluated by H and E staining, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: AjKissR1 is detected in the respiratory tree, ovary, anterior part, and muscle of sea cucumbers.
source: AjKissR1 was detected in the RET, OVA, ANP, and muscle (MUS) (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Significant expression of the kisspeptin precursor is observed in the respiratory tree, testis, and nerve ring in the anterior part sections.
source: Consistent with results from the western blot assay, significant expression of the kisspeptin precursor was observed in the RET, TES, and nerve ring in the ANP sections, with no expression in the MUS and OVA (the inconsistency with results from the western blotting assay vs. immunofluorescence may be due to either differences in the specific structures and components of oocytes or differences in the characteristics of the antibody); AjKissR1 expression was observed in the RET, OVA, MUS and nerve ring in ANP sections, with rare expression in TES (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: AjKissR1 expression is observed in the respiratory tree, ovary, muscle, and nerve ring in anterior part sections, with rare expression in testis.
source: Consistent with results from the western blot assay, significant expression of the kisspeptin precursor was observed in the RET, TES, and nerve ring in the ANP sections, with no expression in the MUS and OVA (the inconsistency with results from the western blotting assay vs. immunofluorescence may be due to either differences in the specific structures and components of oocytes or differences in the characteristics of the antibody); AjKissR1 expression was observed in the RET, OVA, MUS and nerve ring in ANP sections, with rare expression in TES (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The kisspeptin precursor is mainly detected in the coelomic epithelium of the respiratory tree.
source: At the cellular level, the kisspeptin precursor was mainly detected in the coelomic epithelium of RET, whereas AjKissR1 was detected in the brown bodies, which can be found in the luminal spaces of RET and might be related to foreign material removal (Smiley, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and a citation to Smiley, 1994.

claim: AjKissR1 is detected in the brown bodies of the respiratory tree, which might be related to foreign material removal.
source: At the cellular level, the kisspeptin precursor was mainly detected in the coelomic epithelium of RET, whereas AjKissR1 was detected in the brown bodies, which can be found in the luminal spaces of RET and might be related to foreign material removal (Smiley, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and a citation to Smiley, 1994.

claim: Significant expression and cell membrane localization of AjKissR1 is detected in oocytes.
source: In particular, significant expression and cell membrane localization of AjKissR1 was detected in oocytes, indicating the consistent molecular property of AjKissR1 in vivo and in vitro.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Significant fluorescence signal from the kisspeptin precursor, but only a weak signal from AjKissR1, can be detected in spermatogenic epithelium from testis sections.
source: From the TES sections, significant fluorescence signal from the kisspeptin precursor, but only a weak signal from AjKissR1, can be detected in spermatogenic epithelium.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Significant expression of AjKissR1 is detected in the epithelium of muscle from muscle sections.
source: A significant expression of AjKissR1 was detected in the epithelium of muscle from MUS sections.
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The kisspeptin precursor is detectable in the outer surface part of the nerve ring in anterior part sections.
source: Moreover, in the ANP sections, the kisspeptin precursor was detectable in the outer surface part of the nerve ring (mainly containing the cell bodies of neurons, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 F2), whereas the AjKissR1 was detected in the internal region of the nerve ring (mainly containing the axons of neurons, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 F2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2 F2.

claim: AjKissR1 is detected in the internal region of the nerve ring in anterior part sections.
source: Moreover, in the ANP sections, the kisspeptin precursor was detectable in the outer surface part of the nerve ring (mainly containing the cell bodies of neurons, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 F2), whereas the AjKissR1 was detected in the internal region of the nerve ring (mainly containing the axons of neurons, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 F2).
evidence: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2 F2.

claim: The distribution profile of A. japonicus kisspeptin and kisspeptin receptor indicates potential roles of the kiss signaling system in physiological processes such as reproduction, nervous system activity, and metabolism.
source: The distribution profile of A. japonicus kisspeptin and kisspeptin receptor indicates the potential roles of the kiss signaling system in physiological processes, such as reproduction, nervous system activity and metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the tissue distribution data.

claim: Significant ERK phosphorylation signal can be detected by western blot assay in different kisspeptin-treated oocytes.
source: As shown in Figure 7C, significant ERK phosphorylation signal can be detected by western blot assay in different kisspeptin-treated oocytes.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: ERK phosphorylation signal in kisspeptin-treated oocytes can be blocked by the kisspeptin antagonist pep234.
source: This signal can be blocked by the kisspeptin antagonist pep234 (1.0 μM) in DrKiss1-10 or AjKiss1b-10 administrated cells (the inhibitory effect of pep234 was validated in vitro as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 7C and validation data in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Detection by confocal microscopy of the p-ERK signal in treated oocytes demonstrates the activation of the ERK pathway by AjKiss1b-10 and its inhibition by pep234 in A. japonicus cells.
source: Further, detection by confocal microscopy of the p-ERK signal in treated oocytes demonstrated the activation of this pathway by AjKiss1b-10 and its inhibition by pep234 in A. japonicus cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Sea cucumbers treated with AjKiss1b-10 for 40 days exhibit weight loss.
source: Sea cucumbers treated with AjKiss1b-10 for 40 days exhibited weight loss (p=0.0583, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7E) and extremely significant intestinal degeneration (p=0.0001, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7F,G), which are characteristic phenotypes of aestivating A. japonicus (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 7E and a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Sea cucumbers treated with AjKiss1b-10 for 40 days exhibit extremely significant intestinal degeneration.
source: Sea cucumbers treated with AjKiss1b-10 for 40 days exhibited weight loss (p=0.0583, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7E) and extremely significant intestinal degeneration (p=0.0001, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7F,G), which are characteristic phenotypes of aestivating A. japonicus (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo experimental data shown in Figure 7F and G, and a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Weight loss and intestinal degeneration are characteristic phenotypes of aestivating A. japonicus.
source: Sea cucumbers treated with AjKiss1b-10 for 40 days exhibited weight loss (p=0.0583, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7E) and extremely significant intestinal degeneration (p=0.0001, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7F,G), which are characteristic phenotypes of aestivating A. japonicus (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2015.

claim: Extremely significant elevation of transcription of the gene encoding pyruvate kinase (PK) is detected in the respiratory tree of sea cucumbers treated with AjKiss1b-10.
source: Moreover, extremely significant elevation of transcription of the gene encoding pyruvate kinase (PK) (p=0.0002, PBS vs. AjKiss1b-10, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A), which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the regulation of A. japonicus glycolysis (Xiang et al., 2016), was detected in the respiratory tree, whereas a significant decrease of PK transcription was found in the intestine (p=0.0188, PBS vs. AjKiss1b-10, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A and a citation to Xiang et al., 2016.

claim: Pyruvate kinase (PK) is the rate-limiting enzyme in the regulation of A. japonicus glycolysis.
source: Moreover, extremely significant elevation of transcription of the gene encoding pyruvate kinase (PK) (p=0.0002, PBS vs. AjKiss1b-10, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A), which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the regulation of A. japonicus glycolysis (Xiang et al., 2016), was detected in the respiratory tree, whereas a significant decrease of PK transcription was found in the intestine (p=0.0188, PBS vs. AjKiss1b-10, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Xiang et al., 2016.

claim: A significant decrease of PK transcription is found in the intestine of sea cucumbers treated with AjKiss1b-10.
source: Moreover, extremely significant elevation of transcription of the gene encoding pyruvate kinase (PK) (p=0.0002, PBS vs. AjKiss1b-10, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A), which is the rate-limiting enzyme in the regulation of A. japonicus glycolysis (Xiang et al., 2016), was detected in the respiratory tree, whereas a significant decrease of PK transcription was found in the intestine (p=0.0188, PBS vs. AjKiss1b-10, Tukey's multiple comparisons test, as shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4A.

claim: The A. japonicus kisspeptin system plays a role in the control of metabolic balance.
source: These data suggest that the A. japonicus kisspeptin system plays a role in the control of metabolic balance.
evidence: This is an inference based on the in vivo experimental data showing effects on weight, intestinal degeneration, and PK expression.

claim: No significant difference in estradiol (E2) levels in the coelomic fluid of sea cucumber is observed in animals treated with AjKiss1b-10.
source: To evaluate the potential role of AjKiss1b-10 in regulating reproductive activity, we examined the estradiol (E2) levels in the coelomic fluid of sea cucumber, but no significant difference was observed in animals treated with AjKiss1b-10 (Figure 7—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: This is supported by radioimmunoassay data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4B.

claim: AjKissR1/2 expression is detectable in the majority of sea cucumber tissues at all stages, especially after February.
source: At all stages, AjKissR1/2 expression was detectable in the majority of sea cucumber tissues, especially after February (Figure 7H), whereas significant expression of AjpreKiss was found in the ANP from December to April with a peak value detected in February.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: Significant expression of AjpreKiss is found in the anterior part from December to April with a peak value detected in February.
source: At all stages, AjKissR1/2 expression was detectable in the majority of sea cucumber tissues, especially after February (Figure 7H), whereas significant expression of AjpreKiss was found in the ANP from December to April with a peak value detected in February.
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The high expression levels of AjpreKiss during reproductive development suggest its role in the regulation of seasonal reproduction.
source: Taken together, the high expression levels of AjpreKiss during reproductive development suggests its role in the regulation of seasonal reproduction, whereas the wide distribution of AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 in the other tissues investigated indicates diverse functions for these two receptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal expression pattern of AjpreKiss.

claim: The wide distribution of AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 in tissues indicates diverse functions for these two receptors.
source: Taken together, the high expression levels of AjpreKiss during reproductive development suggests its role in the regulation of seasonal reproduction, whereas the wide distribution of AjKissR1 and AjKissR2 in the other tissues investigated indicates diverse functions for these two receptors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the spatial distribution pattern of AjKissR1 and AjKissR2.

claim: The hypothalamic neuropeptide kisspeptin acts as a neurohormone and plays important roles in the regulation of diverse physiological processes in vertebrates.
source: The hypothalamic neuropeptide kisspeptin acts as a neurohormone and plays important roles in the regulation of diverse physiological processes in vertebrates, including reproductive development (Popa et al., 2008; Franssen and Tena-Sempere, 2018), metastasis suppression (Ciaramella et al., 2018), metabolism and development (Song et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2017; Katugampola et al., 2017), behavioral and emotional control (Comninos et al., 2017), and the innate immune response (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Popa et al., 2008; Franssen and Tena-Sempere, 2018; Ciaramella et al., 2018; Song et al., 2014; Jiang et al., 2017; Katugampola et al., 2017; Comninos et al., 2017; and Huang et al., 2018.

claim: A functional kisspeptin signaling system has been demonstrated in the chordate amphioxus.
source: A functional kisspeptin signaling system has been demonstrated in the chordate amphioxus (Wang et al., 2017), and a number of invertebrate kisspeptin genes have been predicted recently (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014; Semmens et al., 2016; Semmens and Elphick, 2017; Suwansa-Ard et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019), however, missing experimental identification of a kisspeptin-type system in non-chordates makes it difficult to determine whether this signaling system has an ancient evolutionary origin in invertebrates or whether it evolved de novo in the chordate/vertebrate lineages.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Missing experimental identification of a kisspeptin-type system in non-chordates makes it difficult to determine whether this signaling system has an ancient evolutionary origin in invertebrates or whether it evolved de novo in the chordate/vertebrate lineages.
source: A functional kisspeptin signaling system has been demonstrated in the chordate amphioxus (Wang et al., 2017), and a number of invertebrate kisspeptin genes have been predicted recently (Mirabeau and Joly, 2013; Elphick and Mirabeau, 2014; Semmens et al., 2016; Semmens and Elphick, 2017; Suwansa-Ard et al., 2018; Chen et al., 2019), however, missing experimental identification of a kisspeptin-type system in non-chordates makes it difficult to determine whether this signaling system has an ancient evolutionary origin in invertebrates or whether it evolved de novo in the chordate/vertebrate lineages.
evidence: This statement reflects the state of knowledge and the rationale for the study.

claim: It is more likely that kisspeptin signaling might have originated from non-chordate invertebrates given the highly conserved intracellular signaling pathway and physiological functions revealed for the A. japonicus kisspeptin system.
source: Given the highly conserved intracellular signaling pathway and physiological functions revealed for the A. japonicus kisspeptin system, it is more likely that kisspeptin signaling might have originated from non-chordate invertebrates.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings of conserved signaling and functions.

claim: Kisspeptin-type receptors were first annotated in the genome of the acorn worm S. kowalevskii and the purple sea urchin S. purpuratus in 2013.
source: In 2013, kisspeptin-type receptors were first annotated in the genome of the acorn worm S. kowalevskii and the purple sea urchin S. purpuratus (Jékely, 2013; Mirabeau and Joly, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jékely, 2013 and Mirabeau and Joly, 2013.

claim: A kisspeptin-type neuropeptide precursor with 149 amino-acid residues was identified in the starfish Asterias rubens, comprising two putative kisspeptin-type peptides, ArKiss1 and ArKiss2.
source: Moreover, a kisspeptin-type neuropeptide precursor with 149 amino-acid residues was identified in the starfish Asterias rubens, comprising two putative kisspeptin-type peptides, ArKiss1 and ArKiss2 (Semmens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Semmens et al., 2016.

claim: In silico analysis of neural and gonadal transcriptomes enabled the virtual discovery of kisspeptins in the sea cucumbers H. scabra and H. glaberrima.
source: Subsequently, in silico analysis of neural and gonadal transcriptomes enabled the virtual discovery of kisspeptins in the sea cucumbers H. scabra and H. glaberrima (Suwansa-Ard et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Suwansa-Ard et al., 2018.

claim: The presence of kisspeptin-type peptides in extracts of radial nerve cords was confirmed by proteomic mass spectrometry in the crown-of-thorns starfish A. planci.
source: Moreover, the presence of kisspeptin-type peptides in extracts of radial nerve cords was confirmed by proteomic mass spectrometry in the crown-of-thorns starfish A. planci (Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Smith et al., 2017.

claim: A 180-residue protein comprising two putative kisspeptin-type peptides has been predicted and a C-terminally amidated peptide GRQPNRNAHYRTLPF-NH2 was confirmed by mass spectrometric analysis of central nerve ring extracts of A. japonicus.
source: Recently, a 180-residue protein comprising two putative kisspeptin-type peptides has been predicted and a C-terminally amidated peptide GRQPNRNAHYRTLPF-NH2 was confirmed by mass spectrometric analysis of central nerve ring extracts of A. japonicus (Chen et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: The truncated peptide AjKiss1b-10 exhibits high activity in eliciting intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in AjKissR1/2-expressing HEK293 cells.
source: In particular, the truncated peptide AjKiss1b-10 exhibited a high activity in eliciting intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in AjKissR1/2-expressing HEK293 cells, whereas the truncated peptides, AjKiss1a-15, AjKiss1a-13, and AjKiss1a-10, failed to activate the receptors.
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: The truncated peptides AjKiss1a-15, AjKiss1a-13, and AjKiss1a-10 fail to activate AjKissR1 and AjKissR2.
source: In particular, the truncated peptide AjKiss1b-10 exhibited a high activity in eliciting intracellular Ca2+ mobilization in AjKissR1/2-expressing HEK293 cells, whereas the truncated peptides, AjKiss1a-15, AjKiss1a-13, and AjKiss1a-10, failed to activate the receptors.
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data.

claim: Alternative cleavage occurs in the kisspeptin peptides of vertebrates.
source: The functional activity of the truncated peptide AjKiss1b-10 is not unusual, considering that alternative cleavage occurs in the kisspeptin peptides of vertebrates (Kotani et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2009); however, the inactivity of AjKiss1a-15, which has been identified from mass spectrometric detection in A. japonicus (Chen et al., 2019), raises more questions about the functional and structural characteristics of this neuropeptide and requires further investigation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kotani et al., 2001 and Lee et al., 2009.

claim: The inactivity of AjKiss1a-15, which has been identified from mass spectrometric detection in A. japonicus, raises questions about the functional and structural characteristics of this neuropeptide.
source: The functional activity of the truncated peptide AjKiss1b-10 is not unusual, considering that alternative cleavage occurs in the kisspeptin peptides of vertebrates (Kotani et al., 2001; Lee et al., 2009); however, the inactivity of AjKiss1a-15, which has been identified from mass spectrometric detection in A. japonicus (Chen et al., 2019), raises more questions about the functional and structural characteristics of this neuropeptide and requires further investigation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing inactivity of AjKiss1a-15 and a citation to Chen et al., 2019.

claim: In the mammalian genome, a single Kiss1 gene produces a mature 54-amino-acid peptide, Kiss-54, which is further proteolytically truncated to 14- and 13-amino-acid carboxyl-terminal peptides, Kiss-14 and Kiss-13, with a common C-terminal decapeptide (Kiss-10) core.
source: In the mammalian genome, a single Kiss1 gene produces a mature 54-amino-acid peptide, Kiss-54, which is further proteolytically truncated to 14- and 13-amino-acid carboxyl-terminal peptides, Kiss-14 and Kiss-13, with a common C-terminal decapeptide (Kiss-10) core (Kotani et al., 2001; Ohtaki et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Kotani et al., 2001 and Ohtaki et al., 2001.

claim: In non-mammalian vertebrates, two paralogous kisspeptin genes, Kiss1 and Kiss2, are present in the genome of teleosts, producing two mature peptides that share the highly conserved Kiss-10 region with mammalian kisspeptin peptides.
source: In non-mammalian vertebrates, two paralogous kisspeptin genes, Kiss1 and Kiss2, are present in the genome of teleosts, producing two mature peptides that share the highly conserved Kiss-10 region with mammalian kisspeptin peptides (Biran et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009; Zmora et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Biran et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2009; and Zmora et al., 2012.

claim: In the sea cucumber A. japonicus, only one kisspeptin gene was annotated and isolated.
source: Unlike mammalian and non-mammalian vertebrates, in the sea cucumber A. japonicus, only one kisspeptin gene was annotated and isolated.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from gene cloning.

claim: The kisspeptin gene in A. japonicus encodes a 180-amino-acid peptide precursor, which is proteolytically cleaved to two mature peptides, consistent with other kisspeptins identified in the phylum Echinodermata.
source: However, sequence analysis revealed that the kisspeptin gene encodes a 180-amino-acid peptide precursor, which is proteolytically cleaved to two mature peptides, consistent with other kisspeptins identified in the phylum Echinodermata (Semmens et al., 2016; Semmens and Elphick, 2017; Smith et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and citations to Semmens et al., 2016; Semmens and Elphick, 2017; and Smith et al., 2017.

claim: Both putative mature peptides of A. japonicus kisspeptin have a C-terminal Leu-Pro-Phe-amide motif, instead of the Arg-Phe-amide motif common in vertebrate kisspeptins.
source: Both putative mature peptides have a C-terminal Leu-Pro-Phe-amide motif, instead of the Arg-Phe-amide motif common in vertebrate kisspeptins, and exhibit a much lower identity with vertebrate kisspeptin sequences.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis.

claim: A. japonicus kisspeptin peptides exhibit much lower identity with vertebrate kisspeptin sequences.
source: Both putative mature peptides have a C-terminal Leu-Pro-Phe-amide motif, instead of the Arg-Phe-amide motif common in vertebrate kisspeptins, and exhibit a much lower identity with vertebrate kisspeptin sequences.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis.

claim: Human, frog, and zebrafish kisspeptins are potent in activating both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2.
source: Our specificity analysis showed that human, frog, and zebrafish kisspeptins, HsKiss1-10, XtKiss1b-10, and DrKiss1-10 and DrKiss2-10, were potent in activating both AjKissR1 and AjKissR2, whereas the human neuropeptide S (HsNPS, as a negative control) showed no potency to activate AjKissR1 or AjKissR2.
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Neuropeptides AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b can potentiate Ca2+ signaling by binding the human kisspeptin receptor HsKiss1R and the zebrafish kisspeptin receptors DrKiss1Ra/b.
source: Likewise, neuropeptides AjKiss1a and AjKiss1b could potentiate Ca2+ signaling by binding the human kisspeptin receptor HsKiss1R and the zebrafish kisspeptin receptors DrKiss1Ra/b, similar to the corresponding active decapeptides.
evidence: This is supported by calcium mobilization assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: This study provides the first experimental data directly confirming the connection between the kisspeptin systems of vertebrates and A. japonicus.
source: This, to our knowledge, is the first experimental data directly confirming the connection between the kisspeptin systems of vertebrates and A. japonicus, therefore proving that this peptide system is present and active in non-chordate deuterostome species.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the cross-reactivity data.

claim: The kisspeptin peptide system is present and active in non-chordate deuterostome species.
source: This, to our knowledge, is the first experimental data directly confirming the connection between the kisspeptin systems of vertebrates and A. japonicus, therefore proving that this peptide system is present and active in non-chordate deuterostome species.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on all the experimental data.

claim: The kisspeptin signaling system that exists in A. japonicus may extend to other taxa in the echinoderm phylum, considering the high conservation of neuropeptides in different echinoderms.
source: Considering the high conservation of the neuropeptides in different echinoderms (Semmens and Elphick, 2017; Zandawala et al., 2017), our findings strongly suggest that the kisspeptin signaling system that exists in A. japonicus may be extend to other taxa in this phylum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and citations to Semmens and Elphick, 2017 and Zandawala et al., 2017.

claim: In teleosts, although both kisspeptin receptors preferentially activate the Gαq-dependent PKC pathway, one of them is also capable of triggering the Gαs-dependent PKA cascade in response to kisspeptin challenge.
source: However, accumulating evidence shows that in teleosts, although both kisspeptin receptors preferentially activate the Gαq-dependent PKC pathway, one of them is also capable of triggering the Gαs-dependent PKA cascade in response to kisspeptin challenge (Ohga et al., 2013; Biran et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ohga et al., 2013 and Biran et al., 2008.

claim: An amphioxus kisspeptin receptor triggers significant PKC but not PKA signaling when stimulated by two kisspeptin-type peptides using heterologous expression in cultured HEK293 cells.
source: Using CRE-Luc and SRE-Luc reporting assays, which help to discriminate between the AC/PKA and PLC/PKC signaling pathways, an amphioxus kisspeptin receptor was shown to trigger significant PKC but not PKA signaling when stimulated by two kisspeptin-type peptides using heterologous expression in cultured HEK293 cells (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Gαq-coupled signaling is highly conserved in the kisspeptin signaling systems from A. japonicus to mammals.
source: Taken together, it is more likely that Gαq-coupled signaling is highly conserved in the kisspeptin signaling systems from A. japonicus to mammals.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing Gαq-dependent signaling in A. japonicus and knowledge of mammalian kisspeptin signaling.

claim: In mammals, the kisspeptin signaling system is essential for HPG axis regulation, leading to reproductive control.
source: In mammals, it is widely established that the kisspeptin signaling system is essential for HPG axis regulation, leading to reproductive control.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian kisspeptin function.

claim: Hypothalamic kisspeptin neurons stimulate pituitary gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons, which express the kisspeptin receptor, providing a neural pathway for the mammalian kisspeptin neuronal system.
source: Furthermore, the hypothalamic kisspeptin neurons have been found to stimulate pituitary gonadotropin-releasing hormone neurons, which express the kisspeptin receptor, providing a neural pathway for the mammalian kisspeptin neuronal system (Oakley et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oakley et al., 2009.

claim: The reproductive function of the kisspeptin system is controversial in teleosts in light of normal reproductive phenotypes observed in fish in the absence of kisspeptins.
source: In non-mammalian species, especially in teleosts, the reproductive function of the kisspeptin system is still controversial in light of the normal reproductive phenotypes observed in fish in the absence of kisspeptins.
evidence: This reflects the state of knowledge about kisspeptin function in teleosts.

claim: A theory has been proposed that nonreproductive functions beyond HPG regulation are the conserved roles of kisspeptins in vertebrates.
source: A new theory has been proposed in which the nonreproductive functions beyond HPG regulation are the conserved roles of kisspeptins in vertebrates (Tang et al., 2015; Nakajo et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2015 and Nakajo et al., 2018.

claim: The seasonal fluctuation of kisspeptin and receptor transcripts, consistent with the reproductive development process, indicates the possible functional involvement of this system in the control of seasonal reproduction in A. japonicus.
source: The seasonal fluctuation of kisspeptin and receptors transcripts, consistent with the reproductive development process, indicates the possible functional involvement of this system in the control of seasonal reproduction in A. japonicus.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal expression data.

claim: The unequally expressed kisspeptin and receptor protein levels in gonads suggest differential functions of the kisspeptin system in different genders of sea cucumber.
source: Interestingly, the unequally expressed kisspeptin and receptor protein levels in gonads, comparatively high kisspeptin precursor level in testis, and high kisspeptin receptor protein levels in ovary tissue demonstrated in our study, suggests differential functions of the kisspeptin system in different genders of sea cucumber.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential expression data in gonads.

claim: The kisspeptin signaling system has a role in regulating metabolic balance and gut function in sea cucumber.
source: Further investigation using both in vivo and in vitro experiments indicated a role for the kisspeptin signaling system in regulating metabolic balance and gut function in sea cucumber.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo and in vitro experimental data.

claim: A role of kisspeptin signaling in the regulation of the VP/OT system may exist in echinoderms, combining the feeding regulatory function of VP/OT-type neuropeptides and the cross-talk between kisspeptin and VP/OT neural systems.
source: Combining the feeding regulatory function of VP/OT-type neuropeptides characterized in echinoderm (Odekunle et al., 2019) and the cross-talk between kisspeptin and VP/OT neural systems (Higo et al., 2016; Seymour et al., 2017; Nakajo et al., 2018), we suggest that a role of kisspeptin signaling in the regulation of the VP/OT system may exist in echinoderms, and the possible interaction between these two systems and an evolutionarily conserved function of the kisspeptin system is worthy of further exploration.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings and citations to Odekunle et al., 2019; Higo et al., 2016; Seymour et al., 2017; and Nakajo et al., 2018.
